paragraphs: Active regression asks which examples should receive labels when obtaining those labels is costly. The learner starts with many unlabeled examples, a collection of candidate models, and access to an oracle that supplies requested labels. Its aim is to reach a specified prediction accuracy while requesting as few labels as possible.

This paper studies that problem when noise varies across examples, a setting called heteroscedastic regression. Rather than treating every observation as equally noisy, the analysis allows the uncertainty in a label to depend on its input. The authors establish convergence-rate bounds for both active learning and passive learning, providing a theoretical basis for comparing their label requirements.

The central finding is that partial knowledge about the noise can substantially improve the label efficiency of active learning. This is a conditional opportunity: the benefit comes from having some information about how noise behaves. The results connect selective labeling in regression to similar gains already recognized in binary classification.
icml-2017-active-heteroscedastic-regress.tldr: Partial knowledge of input-dependent noise can substantially reduce the labels needed for active regression.

paragraphs: Selecting several promising options is different from finding a single winner. This paper studies how to identify K options, or arms, whose average expected reward is close to that of the best K arms. The target is a probabilistic guarantee: with probability at least 1 minus delta, the difference between those averages is at most epsilon.

The authors introduce a hardness parameter that describes the difficulty of an individual problem instance. They then develop two algorithms whose sample requirements depend on this parameter. This makes the analysis sensitive to the particular selection problem, rather than describing every instance through the same worst-case sample requirement.

For a large class of instances, the resulting bounds can be substantially smaller than prior results. In the worst case, they match an instance-independent lower bound except for a logarithmic factor in inverse epsilon. A further lower bound shows that this extra factor is necessary for instance-dependent algorithms using the proposed hardness parameter, clarifying the scope of the improvement.
icml-2017-adaptive-multiple-arm-identifi.tldr: Two algorithms adapt the sampling needed to select several good arms to a new measure of instance difficulty.

paragraphs: A deep network need not spend the same amount of computation on every input. This paper builds on the observation that many examples can be classified correctly with relatively inexpensive computation, while a smaller fraction needs a more costly network. The authors learn policies that allocate evaluation effort separately for each example.

They propose two schemes. One chooses which components of a network to evaluate and lets suitable examples exit at earlier layers. The other chooses which network to run from available alternatives. Both policy-learning problems are expressed through a global objective and reduced to a sequence of weighted binary classification problems, one layer at a time.

The experiments report speedups of up to 2.8 times on ImageNet challenge networks, with less than one percentage point of top-five accuracy loss. Thus, although avoiding accuracy loss motivates the approach, the stated empirical result is a substantial computational saving with a small loss. The contribution is an adaptive way to use networks without requiring their redesign.
icml-2017-adaptive-neural-networks-for-e.tldr: Learned early-exit and network-selection policies reduce inference cost, achieving up to 2.8 times speedup with small reported accuracy losses.

paragraphs: Clustering a changing stream becomes difficult when points have many coordinates and can be deleted as well as inserted. This paper addresses the k-median problem in such streams, with points drawn from a discrete Euclidean grid. Its strategy is to maintain a small weighted summary, called a coreset, instead of retaining the complete point set.

With high probability, the summary approximates the clustering cost for every possible choice of k centers within a factor of 1 plus epsilon. The algorithms have space and time requirements polynomial in dimension and logarithmic coordinate range, multiplied by k and inverse epsilon squared. Previous dynamic-stream algorithms with the stated approximation guarantee required exponential dependence on dimension.

The authors also give versions whose coreset weights are all positive, at the cost of additional logarithmic factors. These summaries support subsequent offline k-median computation. The methods further extend to metric spaces with bounded doubling dimension, showing that the approach is not restricted to the original Euclidean-grid setting.
icml-2017-clustering-high-dimensional-dy.tldr: Small weighted summaries enable accurate k-median clustering of dynamic streams without exponential dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Robotic reinforcement learning must cope with complex, initially unknown dynamics while learning from limited experience. The paper seeks to combine two useful properties: the ability of model-free methods to handle difficult dynamics and the data efficiency of model-based methods. It does so by making their policy updates compatible within a shared framework.

The key choice is to focus on time-varying linear-Gaussian policies. This structure supports a model-based algorithm built around the linear-quadratic regulator, which the authors integrate into path integral policy improvement, a model-free framework. They can also combine the method with guided policy search to train more general parameterized policies, including deep neural networks.

Simulation and real-world experiments show the combined method solving challenging manipulation tasks. Its reported performance is comparable to or better than model-free methods while retaining the sample efficiency of model-based methods. These findings support combining the update strategies for the tested tasks, with the structured policies providing the connection between them.
icml-2017-combining-model-based-and-mode.tldr: Combining model-based and model-free policy updates yields strong manipulation performance while retaining model-based sample efficiency in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a vector from fewer noisy linear measurements than would ordinarily determine it. Success requires prior knowledge about which vectors are plausible. This paper replaces the usual assumption of sparsity in a chosen basis with the assumption that the vector lies near the outputs of a generative model.

The generator maps a k-dimensional input into an n-dimensional vector. If it is L-Lipschitz, meaning its outputs change at a bounded rate as its inputs change, the authors show that roughly order k log L random Gaussian measurements suffice for a Euclidean-norm recovery guarantee. The result ties measurement requirements to the generator's input dimension and regularity.

The authors demonstrate the approach using published variational autoencoder and generative adversarial network models. Their method can achieve the same accuracy as Lasso with five to ten times fewer measurements. This establishes generative models as an alternative source of reconstruction structure, with the theoretical guarantee depending on the stated generator and measurement assumptions.
icml-2017-compressed-sensing-using-gener.tldr: Generative models can replace sparsity assumptions in compressed sensing, with recovery guarantees and reported reductions in measurement requirements.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods work especially well on convex objectives, but non-convex objectives can violate the geometry those methods rely on. This paper develops a variant of Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent that uses this tension constructively. It either makes rapid progress resembling the convex case or produces evidence that the objective is non-convex.

That evidence is a certificate the algorithm can use to exploit negative curvature. Instead of treating the failure of convex-like progress as an unexplained obstacle, the method turns it into information for further optimization. The resulting acceleration is deterministic, and its stated evaluation bounds do not explicitly grow with the dimension.

For functions with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and Hessians, the method finds a point with gradient norm at most epsilon using O(epsilon^(-7/4) log(1/epsilon)) evaluations. A further Lipschitz assumption on the third derivative improves this to O(epsilon^(-5/3) log(1/epsilon)). The guaranteed target is a small gradient, rather than a globally optimal solution.
icml-2017-convex-until-proven-guilty-dim.tldr: An accelerated method either makes convex-like progress or exploits certified non-convexity to reach small-gradient points faster.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks with three-dimensional kernels can jointly model spatial and temporal features in video and volumetric images. The paper identifies a hardware obstacle: GPU memory limits network size, while existing CPU implementations are too slow to provide a practical alternative. Its goal is to make multidimensional convolution efficient on multicore CPUs.

The authors extend Winograd-class convolution algorithms to N dimensions and adapt them to CPU memory behavior. They exploit flexible memory access and inexpensive sparse access to remove the need to handcraft algorithms manually. They also transform data matrices to suit cache use and align their sizes with AVX vector widths, improving processor utilization and multicore scalability.

The reported throughput improvement is five to twenty-five times over the previous state of the art. Two-dimensional convolution is included as a special case and described as the least beneficial case for the approach. The contribution therefore concerns efficient computation across convolution dimensions, with particular motivation from the memory demands of higher-dimensional networks.
icml-2017-deep-tensor-convolution-on-mul.tldr: CPU-optimized multidimensional Winograd convolution delivers reported throughput improvements of five to twenty-five times.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, as when a recommendation system observes which of two items a user prefers. This paper assumes a Condorcet winner: an option that wins against each other option in pairwise preference. It distinguishes strong regret, which vanishes only when both selected options are the winner, from weak regret, which vanishes when either is.

The authors propose Winner Stays variants for both objectives. For N options, the weak-regret version has expected cumulative regret O(N²), improving to O(N log N) when the options have a total order. Crucially, these bounds do not grow with the number of rounds, T.

The strong-regret version adds an O(N log T) term to the corresponding bounds. Thus the two objectives lead to different time dependence even within the same algorithm family. Numerical experiments using simulated and real data report substantially smaller regret than existing algorithms in both settings, while the method remains computationally simple even with many options.
icml-2017-dueling-bandits-with-weak-regr.tldr: Winner Stays achieves expected cumulative weak regret bounded independently of time under the Condorcet-winner assumption.

paragraphs: Gradient descent often trains neural networks successfully even though their optimization problems are non-convex. This paper asks when that success can be proved, rather than only observed. It studies a specific architecture: a network with one hidden layer, non-overlapping convolutional structure, and ReLU activation.

For this architecture, the authors establish a sharp distinction between general inputs and a particular input distribution. Learning is NP-complete in the general case. When inputs follow a Gaussian distribution, however, they prove that gradient descent converges to a global optimum in polynomial time. The distributional assumption is therefore central to the positive result.

The finding shows how a restricted statistical setting can make optimization provably tractable despite worst-case hardness for the same architecture. Its guarantee concerns reaching the global optimum, which is stronger than merely reaching a point with a small gradient. The stated architecture and Gaussian-input condition define the scope of that conclusion; the result does not assert the same behavior for arbitrary convolutional networks.
icml-2017-globally-optimal-gradient-desc.tldr: Gradient descent provably reaches a global optimum in polynomial time for a specific non-overlapping ReLU ConvNet with Gaussian inputs.

paragraphs: Conditional gradient methods, also called Frank-Wolfe methods, are attractive because they rely on a linear optimization oracle. This oracle is a subroutine that solves a linear optimization problem for the algorithm. The surrounding method can be simple even when implementing and repeatedly calling that subroutine is computationally expensive.

This paper proposes a general way to make several conditional gradient algorithms lazy. The method uses a faster separation oracle in place of most linear optimization calls, while retaining a small number of calls to the original oracle. The central change is therefore how the algorithm obtains the information needed to keep progressing.

In actual computations, the authors report wall-clock speedups of several orders of magnitude. The finding highlights a practical distinction between an algorithm's simple description and the cost of its underlying operations. When linear optimization is expensive, reducing dependence on that operation can deliver large runtime improvements. The contribution is a reusable modification for various conditional gradient methods, rather than a single application-specific optimization procedure.
icml-2017-lazifying-conditional-gradient.tldr: Replacing most costly linear optimization calls with a faster separation oracle substantially accelerates several conditional gradient methods.

paragraphs: This paper trains a recurrent neural network to act as an optimizer. Gradient descent is used to train the optimizer on simple synthetic functions. After training, the learned optimizer can tackle derivative-free black-box objectives, where it must search using function evaluations rather than derivatives of the objective being optimized.

The authors report transfer across several kinds of problems: Gaussian process bandits, simple control objectives, global optimization benchmarks, and hyperparameter tuning. This transfer is the central result. Training on synthetic functions produces a search procedure that can be used efficiently on a broader collection of objectives than those used to teach it.

Up to the training horizon, the learned optimizers develop a tradeoff between exploring uncertain possibilities and exploiting promising ones. They also compare favorably with heavily engineered Bayesian optimization packages on hyperparameter tuning. The horizon qualification matters: the stated finding about learned exploration and exploitation applies over that span. The work shows that useful optimization behavior can itself be acquired through training.
icml-2017-learning-to-learn-without-grad.tldr: Recurrent optimizers trained on synthetic functions transfer to diverse derivative-free tasks and learn exploration–exploitation tradeoffs up to their training horizon.

paragraphs: A decision can have several consequences that compete with one another. This paper studies a bandit setting in which each action returns a vector of feedback rather than one reward. The learner seeks a policy that handles the objectives together while accounting for fairness across them.

The authors formalize fairness through the Generalized Gini Index, which aggregates the multiple objectives. They develop an online gradient descent algorithm that uses the convexity of this aggregation function and carefully controls exploration. Their analysis gives a distribution-free regret bound that decreases at approximately the inverse square root of the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors, with high probability.

The method is tested on synthetic data and an electric battery control problem. In the battery application, the competing objectives concern the degradation rates of different cells, and the aim is to balance their use. This example makes the fairness objective concrete: a policy should account for how its effects are distributed across cells, not simply optimize an undifferentiated outcome.
icml-2017-multi-objective-bandits-optimi.tldr: An online bandit algorithm uses the Generalized Gini Index to balance competing objectives with a high-probability regret guarantee.

paragraphs: Kernel quadrature estimates integrals from function values at selected points. Its known root-mean-square convergence rate depends on the integrand's smoothness relative to its dimension. This paper focuses on another part of the error expression: the multiplying constant, which empirical investigation shows can be highly sensitive to how the random points are sampled.

That sensitivity makes the sampling distribution a practical design choice. Unlike optimal importance sampling for standard Monte Carlo integration, the distribution minimizing this constant for kernel quadrature has no closed-form expression. The authors identify choosing a useful sampling distribution as an important open problem and investigate one automatic approach.

Their proposed method combines adaptive tempering with sequential Monte Carlo to select the sampling distribution. Experiments show integration-error reductions of up to four orders of magnitude. The result illustrates how improving point selection can greatly improve practical accuracy even when attention to the convergence-rate exponent alone would miss the opportunity. It is an empirical improvement, rather than a closed-form solution to the optimal-sampling problem.
icml-2017-on-the-sampling-problem-for-ke.tldr: Adaptive sampling for kernel quadrature produces reported integration-error reductions of up to four orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Training a feedforward neural network requires an optimization method that is both effective and affordable to run. This paper develops an efficient block-diagonal approximation to the Gauss-Newton matrix. The approximation provides a structured way to use information beyond the gradients employed by first-order optimization methods.

The resulting algorithm is competitive with leading first-order methods and sometimes delivers substantial optimization improvements. The authors also report that it can perform well with default settings. This matters because tuning optimization parameters for first-order methods can require considerable effort. The claim is that good default performance is possible, rather than that tuning becomes unnecessary in every problem.

A separate theoretical result concerns networks with piecewise linear transfer functions: their objective can have no differentiable local maxima. The authors suggest this may partly explain why such transfer functions support effective optimization. That interpretation remains qualified. Together, the results offer both a practical training algorithm and a structural observation about the objectives associated with these transfer functions.
icml-2017-practical-gauss-newton-optimis.tldr: An efficient block-diagonal Gauss-Newton approximation competes with first-order neural-network optimizers and can work well with default settings.

paragraphs: Identity testing asks whether observations come from a specified reference distribution. This paper studies categorical data when the sample is small and the test must also protect privacy. The task is to distinguish exact agreement with the reference from a difference of at least alpha in total variation distance.

The authors give sample-size bounds that jointly ensure pure differential privacy and specified limits on both kinds of testing error. Those errors correspond to rejecting a correct reference distribution and failing to detect a sufficiently different one. The analysis therefore links the amount of data needed to privacy, separation, and error requirements.

In some parameter regimes, privacy may come without an additional sample-complexity cost. The proposed bounds also improve on applying a chi-squared test to noisy counts or using standard repetition approaches to privatize chi-squared-style statistics. The paper experimentally compares sample requirements with recently proposed private tests. Its contribution is a testing method designed around the privacy constraint while keeping data requirements small.
icml-2017-privit-private-and-sample-effi.tldr: Private identity tests achieve strong sample-efficiency guarantees, with no additional privacy-related sample cost in some parameter regimes.

paragraphs: Sometimes a programmer knows the broad procedure for solving a task but does not know the correct action at every step. This paper provides a way to combine that procedural knowledge with learned behavior. A programmer writes a partial Forth program containing slots whose behavior is learned from input-output examples.

The authors make the interpreter differentiable from end to end, allowing gradient descent to optimize the missing behavior against user-specified objectives. The program can also become part of a larger neural computation graph. This makes explicit program structure and neural learning compatible within a jointly trainable system.

Experiments show that the interpreter can use different amounts of supplied program structure to learn behaviors including sorting sequences and addition. When connected to an LSTM's outputs and trained jointly, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on reasoning about quantities in natural-language stories. The findings support using procedural knowledge as part of the model, particularly when available training data is scarce.
icml-2017-programming-with-a-differentia.tldr: A differentiable Forth interpreter lets programmers supply partial procedures and learn their missing behavior from examples.

paragraphs: Large imperfect-information games are often solved through repeated strategy updates. Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, is a prominent method for zero-sum games of this kind. This paper introduces Best-Response Pruning, a modification that temporarily removes poorly performing actions from consideration during such iterative computation.

The theoretical result identifies which actions the method eventually prunes when combined with CFR in zero-sum games. Asymptotically, it prunes any action that belongs to no best response to any Nash equilibrium. This connects pruning to the game's equilibrium structure, rather than treating a currently disappointing action as permanently irrelevant without justification.

The authors prove faster convergence and lower memory requirements from this modification. Experiments report a sevenfold reduction in space, with the reduction factor increasing as game size grows. The contribution therefore addresses both the time needed for iterative solution methods to converge and the memory needed to run them. The asymptotic characterization explains why removing selected actions can remain compatible with solving the game.
icml-2017-reduced-space-and-faster-conve.tldr: Best-Response Pruning provably accelerates CFR and reduces memory use, with a sevenfold space reduction reported experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of model parameters in high-dimensional single-index models. Its focus is robust estimation when the underlying parameter may have structure and the noise is only minimally restricted. The aim is to obtain statistical guarantees without tying the approach to one narrow form of parameter structure.

The authors propose two families of estimators based on U-statistics. These can be understood as generalizations of several existing algorithms for one-bit compressed sensing. Under suitable conditions, the paper establishes guarantees for recovering structured parameters with these estimators. The minimal noise assumptions are part of that result, but the guarantees still depend on the stated suitable conditions.

The framework is also instantiated for single-index models whose transfer function is monotone. This version is designed to make better use of that monotonicity, incorporating additional known structure into estimation. Experiments support the theoretical analyses. Overall, the contribution combines a broader robust estimation framework with a specialized construction that uses an available property of the model.
icml-2017-robust-structured-estimation-w.tldr: Two U-statistic-based estimator families support robust structured recovery in high-dimensional single-index models under suitable conditions.

paragraphs: Selecting a valuable set is harder when some selected items may later disappear. This paper studies that problem for monotone submodular objectives, where adding items does not reduce value and additional items offer diminishing returns. The selection has a size budget k, and robustness is evaluated against worst-case removal of tau items.

The proposed Partitioned Robust algorithm builds partitions containing buckets whose sizes increase exponentially. It applies standard submodular optimization routines within these buckets to construct the final selection. This organization supports a constant-factor approximation guarantee for tau = o(k), meaning the removal budget grows more slowly than the selection budget.

Earlier work provided the same type of guarantee only for tau = o(sqrt(k)). The new result therefore covers a substantially broader asymptotic range of removals, resolving the stated open problem. Numerical tests on data summarization and influence maximization also show gains over greedy selection and the earlier robust algorithm. Those experiments complement the worst-case guarantee with evidence from the two applications.
icml-2017-robust-submodular-maximization.tldr: Exponentially sized buckets extend constant-factor robust submodular maximization guarantees to removal budgets growing sublinearly with the selection budget.

paragraphs: Kernel online learning combines flexible models with regret guarantees for sequential decisions. First-order methods have relatively low computational costs and optimal square-root regret when convexity is the only available property. Many common losses have additional curvature, however, which second-order methods can use to obtain stronger regret bounds.

The paper introduces kernel online Newton step, or KONS, with regret O(d_eff log T), where d_eff measures the problem's effective dimension. The authors also express an existing kernel determinant-based bound in this form. The obstacle is computation: second-order methods require quadratic time and space in the number of rounds processed.

An adaptive matrix sketch addresses that obstacle by approximating the kernel matrix. With a chosen positive parameter gamma at most one, Sketched-KONS uses O(t² gamma²) time and space per iteration while increasing regret by a factor of 1/gamma. This gives an explicit resource–accuracy tradeoff: a smaller sketch saves computation and memory at a quantified cost in the regret guarantee.
icml-2017-second-order-kernel-online-con.tldr: Adaptive kernel sketching reduces the computational cost of second-order online learning with a quantified increase in regret.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize complex topological properties of shapes and are useful representations for learning. However, their natural comparisons do not directly provide the Hilbert-space structure used by many kernel methods. This paper develops a new kernel to make persistence diagrams easier to incorporate into a learning pipeline.

The construction uses the Sliced Wasserstein approximation to Wasserstein distance. The authors prove both stability and discriminative properties relative to the specified Wasserstein distance between diagrams. These properties address complementary needs: the comparison should tolerate small perturbations while retaining meaningful distinctions between diagrams.

The paper also develops an approximation technique that reduces kernel computation time. Benchmark experiments show favorable comparisons with existing persistence-diagram kernels. The contribution therefore combines mathematical properties of the representation with a way to make its computation more practical. Stability alone is not the entire goal; the stated discrimination guarantee also supports using the kernel to distinguish diagram structure, while the experiments assess its usefulness in learning settings.
icml-2017-sliced-wasserstein-kernel-for-.tldr: A Sliced Wasserstein kernel provides provably stable and discriminative persistence-diagram comparisons, with a faster approximation and favorable benchmark results.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization combines fitting observed data with a penalty that encourages a sparse solution. This paper studies objectives formed from losses over n data points, each with d dimensions, together with a non-convex sparsity penalty. Its contribution concerns the computational difficulty of obtaining approximately optimal solutions for a broad class of such objectives.

The authors prove strong NP-hardness for finding an O(n^c1 d^c2)-optimal solution whenever both exponents lie between zero and one and their sum is less than one. Thus, the hardness result extends beyond exact optimization to the stated family of approximation tolerances. It applies across a broad class of losses and sparse penalties.

The implication is a worst-case barrier: unless P equals NP, a polynomial-time algorithm cannot generally provide those approximation guarantees throughout the covered problem class. The result makes the requested quality of an approximate solution central to the complexity claim. It establishes that allowing approximation at the specified scales does not, by itself, remove the difficulty introduced by these sparse optimization problems.
icml-2017-strong-np-hardness-for-sparse-.tldr: A broad class of non-convex sparse optimization problems remains strongly NP-hard even under the specified approximation tolerances.

paragraphs: Finding Granger-causal relationships among many time series requires more than estimating which relationships are present. Researchers also need to assess the uncertainty of those estimates and manage false discoveries across many tests. This paper addresses both needs in the high-dimensional setting, where existing approaches lacked the stated uncertainty tools.

The first contribution is an asymptotically unbiased estimator of Granger causality, accompanied by test statistics and confidence intervals. Asymptotic unbiasedness describes behavior as the amount of data grows. The associated inferential tools make it possible to attach uncertainty assessments to estimates rather than report only estimated relationships.

The second contribution is a false discovery rate control method that accommodates dependence among both test statistics and observations. The authors report higher multiple-testing power than existing techniques. Experiments on synthetic and climatological data corroborate the theoretical results. Together, the contributions support evaluating individual relationships while also controlling false discoveries across the larger collection of tested relationships.
icml-2017-uncertainty-assessment-and-fal.tldr: A new Granger-causality estimator supplies uncertainty assessments, alongside higher-power false discovery control that accommodates dependent data and tests.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can learn useful visual features, but supervised training depends on substantial labeled data. This paper proposes an end-to-end training framework that uses no supervision. It fixes a collection of target representations, called Noise As Targets, and trains the network's features to align with them.

The fixed targets and alignment constraints are designed to avoid trivial solutions and feature collapse, where the learned representations cease to meaningfully distinguish inputs. A stochastic batch reassignment strategy organizes how examples are matched to targets. Combined with a separable squared loss, this allows the approach to scale to millions of images.

The authors report that the resulting representations perform comparably to leading unsupervised methods on ImageNet and Pascal VOC. The framework is described as domain agnostic, so its training principle does not depend on task-specific supervision. Its significance is that fixed noise targets can support useful representation learning when paired with a training scheme that prevents collapse and remains computationally scalable.
icml-2017-unsupervised-learning-by-predi.tldr: Aligning image features with fixed noise targets enables scalable unsupervised training with competitive reported representation quality.
